category: Ritual formulas, toasts, blessings, and politeness

entries.meaning: A warm, understated thank-you, said for a favor rather than for a gift. Dropping the I makes it sound casual and a little gruff, which is exactly why so many Americans reach for it instead of thank you.
examples: "Here's your coffee." "Hey, appreciate it."
Thanks for covering my shift — really appreciate it.
Appreciate it, man. I'll get you back next week.
He held the door and she nodded. "'Preciate it."
If you could send that over by Friday, much appreciated.

entries.meaning: Thanks that promises a favor back. It is said when someone has gone genuinely out of their way, and it implies a friendly running tally rather than an actual debt.
examples: Thanks for picking me up at the airport — I owe you one.
"I owe you one," he said, sliding the signed form back across the desk.
You really didn't have to stay late for this. I owe you big time.
I owe you one — next round's on me.
If you can get us that reservation, I owe you.

entries.meaning: A tidy written thank-you, at home at the end of an email, a note, or an acknowledgments page. Spoken aloud by an American it sounds a little bookish or a little British; on paper it is completely ordinary.
examples: Many thanks for turning this around so quickly.
"Many thanks, and let me know if anything else comes up."
Many thanks to the volunteers who set up the chairs this morning.
She ended every message the same way: "Many thanks, Ellen."
Many thanks in advance for your help with these forms.

entries.meaning: An old-fashioned thank-you with a courtly, Western flavor. Americans still say it, but mostly older men, Southerners, and anyone deliberately putting on a cowboy voice.
examples: "Much obliged, ma'am," he said, tipping his hat.
Much obliged for the ride into town.
My grandfather never said thanks — it was always "much obliged."
She handed him the wrench and he grunted, "Obliged."
Much obliged, folks. That'll get us through the winter.

entries.meaning: The full, standard expression of gratitude — correct absolutely everywhere, from a cashier to a eulogy, and more sincere-sounding than thanks simply because it takes longer to say. Said flatly with a falling tone it has a second life meaning that is exactly my point.
examples: Thank you — this is the nicest thing anyone's done for me all year.
"Thank you so much for coming," she said at the door.
Thank you, Your Honor.
And that, thank you very much, is why I don't lend him my car.
"Your fries." "Thank you."
See? I was right all along. Thank you.

variants: thank you for your service to our country
entries.meaning: The formula an American says to someone identified as a veteran or an active-duty service member — at an airport gate, at a register offering a military discount, at a Veterans Day assembly. It is barely thirty years old and now close to automatic, and it is worth knowing that a substantial number of veterans find it hollow, embarrassing, or a conversation-ender, and would rather be asked an actual question.
examples: The gate agent saw the cap. "Thank you for your service."
"Thank you for your service, sir. The coffee's on us."
Somebody says thank you for your service to my uncle about once a week and he still never knows what to say back.
The principal shook each of them by the hand: "Thank you for your service."
"Thank you for your service." "I fixed radios in Germany, but thanks."

entries.meaning: The short everyday thank-you — one syllable, low effort, right for anything from a held door to a delivered package. Alone at the bottom of a work email it is perfectly normal; said clipped and flat to someone's face it can read as dismissive.
examples: Thanks! I'll take it from here.
"Two sugars?" "Just one, thanks."
Thanks for the heads-up about the road closure.
She typed "thx" and hit send.
No thanks — I'm driving tonight.
Yeah. Thanks for nothing.

entries.meaning: Literally an intensified thanks, but Americans use it sarcastically about as often as sincerely, and tone does all the work. Bright and quick it is real gratitude; flat, with the weight on lot, it means you have just made my life worse.
examples: Thanks a lot for staying late to help us finish.
"Thanks a lot, you guys. I couldn't have done it without you."
You told her it was my idea? Thanks a lot.
Well, thanks a lot — now I have to start the whole thing over.
He read the review, muttered "thanks a lot," and shut his laptop.

entries.meaning: A friendly, exaggerated thank-you for a real favor. Thanks a million is nearly always sincere, while thanks a bunch tips into sarcasm about as easily as thanks a lot does.
examples: Thanks a million, Rosa — you saved the whole presentation.
"Thanks a ton for the recommendation. I got the job."
Got the tickets. Thanks a million!
Thanks a bunch for warning me the floor was wet.
She waved from the car — "Thanks a million!" — and pulled out of the driveway.

entries.meaning: The scripted thing to say while unwrapping a gift — a modest protest that functions as thanks. Nobody says it literally, and nobody is expected to take the gift back.
examples: "You shouldn't have!" she said, already tearing the paper off.
Flowers? You really shouldn't have.
He handed her the little box. "Oh, you shouldn't have."
You shouldn't have — but I'm very glad you did.
They gave him a retirement plaque with his name misspelled. You shouldn't have.

entries.meaning: A gracious deflection of a compliment or a generous gesture, meaning roughly that is more than I deserve. It is sincere in courtly mouths and dryly amused when the praise is obviously over the top.
examples: "That was the best talk of the whole conference." "You're too kind."
You're too kind — I really just showed up and read the slides.
He gave a small bow. "Too kind, ladies and gentlemen."
She sent lunch for the entire office. You're too kind.
"You're too kind," he said, pocketing the check anyway.

entries.meaning: A relaxed reply to thanks that means ask me again whenever you want. It is warmer than no problem and works with friends, neighbors, and coworkers, but it sounds too familiar coming from someone serving a stranger.
examples: "Thanks for the jump start." "Anytime."
Anytime, man. Just text me.
"You're a lifesaver." "Anytime — seriously."
She smiled and said anytime, and she meant it.
Anytime you need another set of eyes on it, say the word.

entries.meaning: An offer of help delivered with a flourish, and a courtly way of answering thanks. It is straight-faced in hotels and fine restaurants; everywhere else it is friendly theater, usually tacked onto your own name.
examples: "Are you the one who fixed the projector?" "At your service."
"Dave Ramirez, at your service."
The concierge nodded. "At your service, ma'am."
Need a ride to the airport at five in the morning? At your service.
He swept off an imaginary hat. "At your service."

entries.meaning: A modest answer to thanks, meaning the favor was too small to be worth thanking anyone for. It is slightly old-fashioned and faintly gallant, and it can carry a joking undertone of let us never speak of this again.
examples: "Thank you for dinner." "Don't mention it."
Don't mention it — you'd have done the same for me.
He waved her off. "Don't mention it. Really."
"I owe you." "Don't mention it. Ever."
Don't mention it; it took me all of five minutes.

entries.meaning: A wave of the hand that answers a thank-you, an apology, or an offer to pay you back. It is generous when warm and conversation-ending when flat, and it is one of the most common things Americans say instead of you're welcome.
examples: "I'm so sorry I'm late." "Don't worry about it, we just sat down."
Don't worry about it — I'll cover the check this time.
"I still owe you twenty bucks." "Don't even worry about it."
He broke a glass and the bartender said, "Don't worry about it, happens every night."
"Should I call and explain?" "Don't worry about it. It's handled."

entries.meaning: The workplace and service-industry standard reply to thanks — friendly, professional, and safe with customers, where no problem can sound too loose. It also works before the fact, as an offer.
examples: "Thanks for walking me through it." "Happy to help!"
Glad to help — call back if it starts doing that again.
Let me know if you get stuck; happy to help.
"Happy to," she said, already reaching for the box.
No trouble at all — happy to help.

entries.meaning: A gracious reply to thanks, standard in hospitality and upscale service and common in polite professional email. Between close friends it lands as either very courtly or lightly sarcastic.
examples: "Thank you for a wonderful evening." "My pleasure."
"My pleasure, sir. Enjoy your stay with us."
Thanks again for the introduction. — My pleasure; I think you two will get along.
"It was my pleasure," she said, and clearly meant it.
"Thanks for the ride." "Pleasure's all mine."

entries.meaning: The most common casual American reply to thanks, and also a way to wave off an apology or agree to a request. Mind the generation gap: to anyone under about fifty it simply means you're welcome, but some older speakers hear it as implying the favor might have been a problem.
examples: "Thanks for grabbing that." "No problem."
Sorry I'm late. — No problem, we just started.
Can you get it to me by five? — No problem.
He shrugged. "No problem, happens all the time."
She texted back a single "np."

entries.meaning: A breezy no problem that insists the favor cost you no effort whatsoever. It peaked in the 1970s and 80s and now sounds a shade older and a shade more swaggering than no problem, and it answers a request as readily as it answers thanks.
examples: "Thanks for hauling all that up three flights." "No sweat."
Can you swing by and grab the keys? — No sweat.
"Sorry, I know it's short notice." "No sweat. I wasn't doing anything anyway."
He wiped his hands on his jeans. "No sweat. Call me if it leaks again."
No sweat — I'll have the whole thing rewired by Friday.

entries.meaning: Australian in origin and now thoroughly at home in American English, especially with younger speakers. It answers both thank you and sorry, and it works on its own as reassurance that nothing is wrong.
examples: "Sorry, I didn't see you there." "No worries."
No worries — I'll just catch the next train.
"Thanks for waiting." "No worries at all."
If you can't make it tonight, no worries.
He replied "no worries" and put his phone face down.

entries.meaning: A polite, slightly formal reply to thanks or to an apology, meaning the trouble was nonexistent. In American mouths it sounds faintly British and rather courtly; younger Americans say no problem instead almost every time.
examples: "Thank you so much for making room for us." "Not at all."
Am I keeping you? — Not at all, please sit down.
"Not at all," the professor said. "I'm glad you asked."
I hope this isn't an imposition. — Not at all.
"Sorry to bother you." "Not at all — what can I do for you?"

entries.meaning: As an answer to thanks it means there was never any question I would do it, and it has quietly become the default for younger Americans who find you're welcome stiff and no problem careless. It is warm, it is safe with customers and strangers, and it does ordinary duty as an emphatic yes besides.
examples: "Thanks for holding my spot in line." "Of course."
"Of course," the nurse said. "That's what we're here for."
Could you send me that file again? — Of course, one second.
"It meant a lot that you came." "Of course I came."
She says of course where her mother would have said you're welcome.

entries.meaning: A breezy formula that answers either a thank-you or a request: after thanks it means you're welcome, and after a favor asked it means yes, I'll do it. It is friendly and very American, and it belongs in speech rather than writing.
examples: "Thanks for locking up." "Sure thing."
Could you grab the mail while we're gone? — Sure thing.
"Sure thing, boss. Give me ten minutes."
"Two coffees?" "Sure thing, coming right up."
He said sure thing and hung up before I could explain the rest.

entries.meaning: A courtly dismissal of thanks, meaning the favor cost you nothing at all. It is genuinely old-fashioned now — you hear it from older speakers, in period pieces, and from people being grandly and deliberately gracious.
examples: "I can't thank you enough." "Think nothing of it."
Think nothing of it, my dear — it was on my way.
He gave a small bow. "Think nothing of it."
"You paid for all of us?" "Think nothing of it."
Think nothing of it. I had the whole afternoon free anyway.

entries.meaning: A hearty Midwestern and Western reply that answers thank you with of course and answers a question with an emphatic yes. You betcha is the folksier form, and outside the Upper Midwest it can sound like a put-on.
examples: "Thanks for the help with the fence." "You bet."
Are you coming to the game? — You bet I am.
"You betcha," she said. "Wouldn't miss it for anything."
Can you hold the elevator? — You bet.
"Appreciate it." "You bet. Anytime."

entries.meaning: A quick, cheerful consider it done that doubles as an answer to thanks. It is diner-counter and hardware-store American — the server taking your order and the coworker you just asked for a favor both reach for it — and it lives in speech, essentially never in writing.
examples: "Can I get a refill over here?" "You got it."
"Thanks for covering the phones." "You got it."
You got it, boss. Eight two-by-fours, cut to six feet.
"Don't mention I told you." "You got it."
He gave a thumbs-up through the kitchen window. "You got it!"

entries.meaning: The standard, unmarked answer to thank you — never wrong anywhere, and the safest thing a learner can memorize. Said pointedly to someone who did not thank you, it becomes a sharp little reproach. Do not confuse it with plain welcome, which greets an arrival.
examples: "Thanks for the ride." "You're welcome."
You're very welcome — I'm glad it worked out.
She said you're welcome to every single person coming through the line.
I fixed your printer, by the way. You're welcome.
"You saved me an entire afternoon." "You're welcome. It was nothing."

entries.meaning: Said while yielding a doorway, an elevator, a buffet line, or a turn — an offer to let the other person go first. It is one of the few politeness formulas that essentially always comes with a gesture.
examples: He held the door and stepped aside. "After you."
"After you," she said, waving him toward the elevator.
Please, after you — I insist.
"Who's up next?" "After you. I'm still stretching."
After you, ladies.

entries.meaning: Permission granted with a shrug: go ahead, it costs me nothing. It can be genuinely hospitable, but very often it carries a dry undertone of if you think you can do better, try it.
examples: "Mind if I take the last slice?" "Be my guest."
You want to tell him yourself? Be my guest.
"Can I use your charger?" "Be my guest — it's on the counter."
If you'd rather explain the budget to the board, be my guest.
Be my guest, but I'd wear boots if I were you.

entries.meaning: A formal apology, a formal request for a repeat, or — with a rising, indignant tone — an objection meaning how dare you. That third sense is the one you will actually hear most often in American English.
examples: I beg your pardon — I didn't mean to interrupt.
"Beg your pardon? I didn't catch that last part."
I beg your pardon! That is absolutely not what I said.
"Begging your pardon, sir, but the car's out front."
He stepped on her foot and mumbled, "Beg your pardon."

entries.meaning: Enthusiastic permission — yes, absolutely, go ahead. It is more gracious than sure, and it turns up in meetings, in email, and wherever a host wants to sound generous rather than merely willing.
examples: "May I ask a question?" "By all means."
By all means, take as much time as you need.
"Should I bring my brother?" "By all means — the more the merrier."
If you'd like to see the garden, by all means, go on out.
"By all means, sit," she said, pulling out a chair.

entries.meaning: The workhorse of American politeness: it gets a stranger's attention, apologizes for a small physical intrusion, asks someone to repeat themselves, covers a burp or a sneeze, and — with a sharp rising tone — challenges something rude.
examples: Excuse me, do you know what time the museum closes?
Excuse me — I just need to squeeze past you.
"Excuse me? Could you say that one more time?"
Excuse me! That's the second time you've cut in line.
He burped, then said "Excuse me" to nobody in particular.
Excuse us, we're trying to get through with a stroller.

entries.meaning: A joking apology for swearing, dropped in just before or just after the word itself. The joke is very old and everybody knows it, and it does not actually make the profanity acceptable in a room where profanity is not.
examples: That was, excuse my French, a complete disaster.
"Pardon my French, but the man is an idiot."
He glanced at his mother. "Excuse my French, Ma."
The whole thing is screwed — excuse my French — from top to bottom.
"Excuse my French." "You said that after, not before."

entries.meaning: A crisp, businesslike apology, most at home in email and professional speech. It sits a notch cooler than I'm sorry, which makes it useful when you want to own a mistake without sounding wounded about it.
examples: My apologies for the delayed reply — I was out of the office all week.
Apologies, everyone; the projector is being difficult again.
"My apologies," the manager said. "That should never have happened."
My sincere apologies to anyone who was kept waiting.
I sent the wrong version of the file. My apologies.

entries.meaning: A casual admission of fault that came out of pickup basketball in the 1980s and spread everywhere. It is friendly and low-stakes; using it for anything genuinely serious makes it sound like you are not taking it seriously.
examples: "You took my charger." "Oh — my bad."
My bad, I thought the meeting was at three.
He knocked over the cup and said "my bad" without looking up.
My bad on the typo in that last email.
"Wrong turn again?" "My bad."

entries.meaning: A disclaimer bolted onto something rude, either just before or just after saying it. Everyone knows it does not actually neutralize the insult, and the expected answer is none taken.
examples: No offense, but that shirt is a lot.
"Your handwriting is completely unreadable. No offense."
No offense to anyone in this room, but this meeting could have been an email.
"No offense." "None taken."
She said no offense three times in one sentence, which is never a good sign.

entries.meaning: The scripted answer to no offense, granting that you are not insulted. It is often a polite fiction, and said flatly or after a pause it signals the exact opposite.
examples: "No offense." "None taken."
None taken — you're not wrong about the shirt.
"No offense to anyone in accounting." "None taken," said the accountant.
He shrugged. "None taken. I've heard a lot worse."
"I hope that didn't come out badly." "None taken, honestly."

entries.meaning: A short, slightly formal excuse me. With rising intonation it asks for a repeat; with falling intonation it apologizes for brushing past someone or for some small breach of manners.
examples: "Pardon? I didn't hear you."
Pardon me — is this seat taken?
He squeezed down the row whispering "Pardon, pardon."
Pardon me for asking, but how much did a place like this run you?
"Pardon me, ma'am, you dropped your glove."
Pardon? He did what?

entries.meaning: The word that turns an order into a request; leaving it out is the fastest way for a learner to sound rude in English. Said alone with a falling tone it has a second sense entirely — stop it, or I don't believe you for a second.
examples: Two coffees, please.
Could you please turn that down?
"Please," she said. "Just hear me out."
Please. He has never once been on time in his life.
Pretty please? With a cherry on top?
"Would you like a bag?" "Yes, please."

entries.meaning: The default apology, stretching from a bumped shopping cart to a death in the family. Two of its uses are not apologies at all: sorry? with a rising tone asks for a repeat, and I'm sorry, but... introduces a flat disagreement with no regret in it whatsoever.
examples: Sorry! I didn't see you standing there.
I'm so sorry about your dad. He was a good man.
"Sorry? Say that one more time."
I'm sorry, but that is simply not what the contract says.
Sorry about that — the line was longer than I expected.
"Sorry, wrong number."

entries.meaning: A warning label bolted to the front of a disagreement, usually aimed at someone senior to you. It sounds deferential and functions as the opposite: every American who hears it braces for the criticism coming right behind it.
examples: With all due respect, sir, that timeline isn't realistic.
"With all due respect, Senator, you didn't answer the question."
With all due respect to the previous speaker, the numbers say otherwise.
"With all due respect —" "Here we go."
No disrespect, but I've been doing this job for twenty years.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French and said to people about to eat — American English never developed a native equivalent, which is why this one stuck. It carries a touch of ceremony, so at a backyard cookout most Americans say dig in instead.
examples: She set the plates down and said, "Bon appétit."
Bon appétit, everybody — don't wait for me.
The waiter poured the wine, wished us bon appétit, and disappeared.
"Here you go. Bon appetit." "It's a hot dog, Kevin."
Bon appétit! Save room for dessert.

entries.meaning: The formula for admitting someone through a door — the answer to a knock, and the first thing a host says to a guest. Doubling it is warmer and hurries the person in out of the cold.
examples: There was a knock, and she called, "Come in!"
Come on in — the door's unlocked.
"Come in, come in. You must be freezing out there."
Come in and shut the door behind you, please.
He knocked twice on the doorframe. "Come in," said the doctor without looking up.

entries.meaning: The plain American start eating, said by a host once the food is on the table. It is casual and hearty, and its real function is to release everyone from politely waiting.
examples: All right, everybody — dig in.
"Dig in before it gets cold."
She set the platter in the middle of the table. "Dig in."
Don't stand on ceremony. Dig in.
Dig in, boys. There's plenty more on the stove.

entries.meaning: A push to start eating and to keep going — warmer and more insistent than dig in, and strongly associated with grandmothers, church basements, and anyone who thinks you look thin. It is an order in form only.
examples: "Eat up, there's a whole other pan in the oven."
Eat up — we're leaving in twenty minutes.
She kept refilling his plate. "Eat up, you're skin and bones."
Eat up, boys, before it goes cold.
"Eat up, now," my grandmother said, and it was not a suggestion.

entries.meaning: What an American server says while setting down a plate, and what anyone says handing over something pleasant. It is used with no object at all, which is what makes it a formula rather than an ordinary verb.
examples: "One veggie burger, no onions. Enjoy!"
Here's your ticket — enjoy the show.
Enjoy, and let me know what you think of the ending.
She handed him the paperback. "Enjoy."
"Enjoy your meal." "You too — I mean, thanks."

entries.meaning: A host's standing permission to take food, drink, or anything else on offer without asking again. It is the usual American way to open a buffet, a fridge, or a snack table to a guest.
examples: "Help yourself — there's more in the kitchen."
Coffee's on the counter; help yourselves.
Help yourself to whatever's in the fridge.
"Can I have one?" "Help yourself."
There's a whole box of them by the door — help yourself.

entries.meaning: A host's blanket invitation to relax and treat the place as your own. It is warm, completely standard, and usually said within the first minute of somebody walking in.
examples: "Come in, make yourself at home. I'll be right back."
Make yourselves at home — bathroom's down the hall on the left.
"Make yourself at home," he said, clearing a pile of laundry off the couch.
Make yourself at home, but please don't touch the thermostat.
"Make yourself at home." "Careful what you offer — I'm a fridge person."

entries.meaning: Said while pouring or serving, asking the other person to call out at the moment they have enough. The scripted answer is the single word when, which is what makes it a ritual rather than a real question.
examples: He tipped the bottle over her glass. "Say when."
"Say when." "When! That's plenty."
Say when — I have no idea how much cheese you want.
She kept pouring, waiting for him to say when.
"Say when," the bartender said, and then just kept going.

entries.meaning: A toast that tells everyone to drain the glass — the bottom of the glass goes up as you tip it back. It is jovial and a little rowdy, and it does joking duty for medicine and anything else you would rather swallow fast.
examples: "Bottoms up!" he said, and the whole table drank.
All right — bottoms up, and then we're switching to water.
She held up the shot glass. "Bottoms up."
He looked at the cough syrup, sighed, and said, "Bottoms up."
Bottoms up, everyone. Last call was ten minutes ago.

entries.meaning: The standard American toast, said as glasses are raised and clinked. Under British influence it has picked up two more jobs here — a light thanks, and a casual email sign-off — both of which sound faintly Anglophile coming from an American.
examples: "Cheers!" Glasses clinked all around the table.
Cheers to the happy couple.
"Here's your change." "Cheers."
Let me know if you need anything else. Cheers, — Dan
He raised his beer an inch off the bar. "Cheers, man."

entries.meaning: Agreement dressed up as a toast — you are endorsing what somebody just said strongly enough to raise a glass to it. It works with or without an actual drink in your hand.
examples: "To never working another weekend." "Cheers to that!"
Whoever invented the four-day week deserves a statue. — Cheers to that.
Cheers to that, brother.
"May this be the last time we ever move apartments." "I'll drink to that."
She lifted her coffee mug. "Cheers to that."

entries.meaning: A jokey toast said right before swallowing something in one go — the hatch being your throat, in old nautical humor. Like bottoms up, it moonlights as what you say to unpleasant medicine.
examples: "Down the hatch!" he said, tossing back the shot.
She plugged her nose. Down the hatch.
One more spoonful — down the hatch.
Down the hatch, and let's never order that again.
He raised the glass to the whole room. "Down the hatch."

entries.meaning: A toast made famous by Casablanca in 1942 and now essentially a quotation. Americans say it over a raised glass with a knowing smile, usually as a small piece of movie cosplay.
examples: He raised his glass across the table. "Here's looking at you, kid."
Here's looking at you — thirty years and still standing.
"Here's looking at you, kid," she said, doing a terrible Bogart.
Here's looking at you, old friend.
They clinked their paper cups. "Here's looking at you."

entries.meaning: An old drinking toast whose origin nobody agrees on — trench mud, racetrack mud, or farm mud, depending on who is telling it. It survives mainly as a deliberately old-timey thing to say when glasses come together.
examples: "Here's mud in your eye!" my grandfather said before every first sip.
He lifted his glass. "Here's mud in your eye."
Here's mud in your eye, and many more.
"What kind of toast is that?" "An old one. Here's mud in your eye."
Here's mud in your eye, boys — we made it through another season.

entries.meaning: The all-purpose American toast frame: here's to plus whoever or whatever you are honoring. Said on its own as here's to you, it salutes the person standing in front of you.
examples: Here's to you, Coach. We wouldn't have made it without you.
"Here's to twenty-five years," he said, raising his glass.
Here's to the ones who couldn't be here tonight.
Here's to us — nobody else would put up with us.
She stood, glass in hand. "Here's to new beginnings."

entries.respell: luh-KHYME (the kh is a throat-clearing sound), also luh-HYME
entries.meaning: Hebrew for to life — the standard Jewish toast, widely recognized in American English through Jewish communities and Fiddler on the Roof. Many American speakers simplify the guttural opening of the second syllable to a plain h.
examples: "L'chaim!" the whole table answered, glasses up.
L'chaim — to life, and to the bride and groom.
He poured two fingers of slivovitz and said, "L'chaim."
L'chaim, Bubbe. Ninety-five years.
The rabbi raised his cup. "L'chaim."

entries.meaning: The German toast, used in American English at Oktoberfest, in German restaurants, and by anyone holding a very large beer and enjoying themselves. It means roughly may it do you good.
examples: "Prost!" The steins came together with a thud.
Prost, everybody — happy Oktoberfest.
He hoisted the liter mug. "Prost!"
Prost! And now somebody please help me carry this thing.
She learned exactly two German words in Munich: danke and prost.

entries.meaning: Spanish for health, used as a toast wherever Spanish and English mix in the United States, which is nearly everywhere. In Spanish it also answers a sneeze, though speaking English most Americans stick with bless you.
examples: "Salud!" they said, touching bottles.
Salud, amigos — to a good harvest.
He raised his margarita. "Salud."
Salud, and thank you all for coming out tonight.
Her grandmother says salud every time anybody sneezes.

entries.meaning: The Scandinavian toast, from an old word for bowl or drinking cup. In America you hear it at Scandinavian-heritage gatherings across the Upper Midwest — and, in a completely separate life, as the chant of Minnesota Vikings fans.
examples: "Skol!" everyone shouted, and drank.
Skål, and God jul.
He lifted the aquavit. "Skol, cousin."
Fifty thousand people chanting "Skol!" in unison is a strange thing to hear.
Skol to Grandma Ingrid, who made every single one of these cookies.

entries.meaning: Irish (and Scottish Gaelic) for health, and the standard Irish toast — heard in American bars every March and wherever Irish Americans raise a glass. The spelling defeats nearly everyone, which is why bartenders say it out loud first.
examples: "Sláinte!" they said, and the pints came together.
Sláinte — to Grandpa Sean, who would have loved every minute of this.
He raised the whiskey. "Sláinte."
The bartender made the whole table say sláinte before anybody drank.
Sláinte, and happy St. Patrick's Day to you.

entries.meaning: The full, formal English toast that all the borrowed ones — salud, prost, skål — translate to. It sounds slightly grand in American English, which is why it shows up at weddings and retirement dinners rather than in bars.
examples: "To your health," he said, and everyone drank.
To your health, and to a long and happy retirement.
She raised her glass to the guest of honor. "Your very good health, sir."
To your health — and to whoever's driving us home tonight.
"What am I supposed to say back?" "Just 'to your health.'"

variants: all the best to you and yours
entries.meaning: A broad, warm good wish, most common as a written sign-off and as the last thing you say to someone who is leaving. Because it sounds like a send-off, it can read as a goodbye even when you did not mean one.
examples: All the best in the new job — they're lucky to have you.
"All the best," she wrote, and signed her name.
All the best to you and the family this holiday season.
He shook my hand at the door. "All the best."
All my best — and don't be a stranger.

entries.meaning: A more finished, slightly more formal good luck, common in email sign-offs and in send-offs where you may not see the person again. Delivered flatly about something doomed, it turns sarcastic like everything else in this category.
examples: Best of luck on Thursday — you're going to do great.
Best of luck in the new role, and please keep in touch.
"Best of luck to you," the interviewer said, shaking his hand.
You're going to ask him to reschedule the whole quarter? Best of luck.
Best of luck, everyone. Results go up at noon.

entries.meaning: The standard American answer to a sneeze — automatic, expected, and only faintly religious anymore. A second sense, said to someone who has just done you a kindness, means roughly you are an angel.
examples: She sneezed twice. "Bless you."
"Bless you." "Thanks — allergies."
He brought me coffee at six in the morning. Bless you.
Bless you, whoever labeled this box.
"Bless you," said three separate strangers on the subway.

entries.meaning: A Southern formula with two faces. Said warmly and to your face it is genuine affection or sympathy; said in the third person about someone who has just done something foolish, it is a polite insult — and every Southerner hears the difference instantly.
examples: "You drove all this way for me? Bless your heart."
He tried to fix the sink himself. Bless his heart.
Bless your heart, honey, you must be exhausted.
She's been telling that same story for thirty years, bless her.
My aunt can say bless your heart in a tone that strips paint.

entries.meaning: Theater's superstitious way of wishing good luck, since saying good luck in a theater is thought to jinx the show. It has spread well past the stage to auditions, interviews, and any nerve-racking appearance.
examples: "Break a leg out there!" the stage manager whispered.
Break a leg at the audition tomorrow.
"Break a leg," she texted him ten minutes before his interview.
He hugged his daughter backstage. "Break a leg, kid."
You never say good luck in a theater — you say break a leg.

entries.meaning: A wish for luck named after the old gesture of crossing your index and middle fingers. It can be a wish aimed at someone else or a statement of your own hope about something still up in the air.
examples: Fingers crossed — we hear back about the house tomorrow.
"Fingers crossed for you on Monday."
The first test came back clean, and the second one, fingers crossed, will too.
Fingers crossed this flight actually leaves on time.
She held up both hands. "Fingers crossed."

entries.meaning: German for health, and the standard secular alternative to bless you after a sneeze. It is fully naturalized in American English and carries no religious weight at all, which is exactly why some people prefer it.
examples: "Achoo!" "Gesundheit."
Gesundheit — that was a big one.
He sneezed into his elbow and somebody in the back said "Gesundheit."
"Bless you." "Gesundheit." "Thank you both."
My mother says gesundheit, my father says bless you, and nobody knows why.

entries.meaning: The standard American wish for someone who is sick — printed on cards, written on a group signature, said at the door of a sickroom. In actual speech feel better is far more common; get well soon sounds like the card it came from.
examples: Get well soon! The whole team signed the card.
"Feel better," he said, leaving the soup on the porch.
Get well soon — the office is chaos without you.
She texted "feel better soon" with a picture of the dog.
"Get well, and don't come back in here until you're not contagious."

entries.meaning: A short blessing used as a farewell, a thank-you, or an expression of fond exasperation about somebody. Its religious force varies enormously from speaker to speaker — for many Americans it now lands closer to take care.
examples: "Thank you for everything. God bless."
God bless — drive safe, now.
He's eighty-four and still shovels his own driveway, God bless him.
"God bless you," she said, pressing the money into his hand.
Good night, everybody, and God bless.

entries.meaning: A small blessing tucked in right after naming someone who has died. It is nearly automatic in older, Catholic, and Southern speech, and it marks respect rather than making any real theological claim.
examples: My father, God rest his soul, never trusted a bank in his life.
"Aunt Rita — God rest her soul — made this every single Easter."
He learned the trade from old Mr. Kowalski, God rest him.
God rest his soul, the man would have hated all this fuss.
She mentions her husband, God rest his soul, in almost every conversation.

entries.meaning: The default American wish for a good outcome — safe in every register, spoken or written. Watch the fixed phrase good luck with that, which almost always means that will never work and I want no part of it.
examples: Good luck on your exam!
"Good luck," the nurse said. "You'll do just fine."
Good luck to both teams tonight.
You're asking him for a raise this week? Good luck with that.
Good luck, and let us know how it goes.

entries.meaning: Said immediately after mentioning your own good fortune, to keep from jinxing it — usually while actually rapping your knuckles on something wooden. It is the most-used superstition formula in American speech, and even confirmed skeptics say it.
examples: I haven't been sick all winter — knock on wood.
"Knock on wood," he said, tapping the table twice.
The car's been running fine, knock wood.
We've never had a flood on this street. Knock on wood.
Knock on wood, but I think we might actually finish early.

entries.meaning: The reflexive answer that hands a good wish straight back, and the safe response to any holiday greeting you were not expecting. Said sharply after an insult, it hands that back too.
examples: "Happy new year!" "Same to you!"
"Have a good one." "Same to you."
Same to you and yours — merry Christmas.
She wished him luck on the exam, and he said same to you.
"Drive safe." "Same to you, and text me when you're home."
"Go jump in a lake." "Same to you, pal."

entries.meaning: The formal expression of sympathy after a death — standard in cards, at funeral homes, and in professional messages. In casual speech most Americans say I'm so sorry instead, and using condolences with a close friend can sound stiff.
examples: "My condolences," he said, shaking her hand at the door.
Please accept our deepest condolences on the loss of your mother.
Condolences to the whole family.
She wrote a short note — just my condolences and a memory of him at the lake.
The entire department sends its condolences.

entries.meaning: The clipped, casual congratulations — right for texts, comments, and hallway conversation, and too breezy for a card, a speech, or anything printed. The gaming forms grats and gratz stay online.
examples: Congrats on the new job!
"Congrats, you two!" she wrote under the photo.
Just heard about the baby — congrats, man.
Congrats to everybody who finished the race today.
He texted "congrats" and a picture of a cake.

entries.meaning: The full formula for marking somebody else's achievement or good news — a degree, a promotion, an engagement, a baby. Said flatly to someone who is bragging, it becomes a dry insult.
examples: Congratulations! We're so happy for you both.
Congratulations on twenty-five years with the company.
"Congratulations, Doctor," he said, handing her the diploma.
Congratulations are in order — she passed the bar.
So you finally did the dishes. Congratulations.

entries.meaning: The fixed wish for a wedding anniversary, extended freely to work anniversaries and to the anniversary of anything worth marking. Like happy birthday it takes happy and nothing else, and it is normally addressed to the couple together rather than to one half of it.
examples: Happy anniversary! Forty years is no small thing.
"Happy anniversary, you two," he said, setting the champagne on the table.
She left a card propped against the coffee maker: Happy anniversary.
Happy anniversary to Denise — ten years with the firm this month.
"It's the fifteenth." "Oh. Happy anniversary." "You forgot again."

entries.meaning: The fixed American birthday formula — said, sung, written on cake, and posted by the hundred on social media. There is no alternative: congratulations on your birthday is not something Americans say.
examples: Happy birthday! Make a wish.
"Happy birthday, Grandpa," the kids shouted into the phone.
Happy birthday to my favorite person — twenty-nine again, I hear.
He posted "HBD" on her wall and figured that covered it.
Happy birthday, and many more.

entries.meaning: The inclusive American winter greeting, covering Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa, and New Year's in one phrase. It is the default in retail, in offices, and in mail to people whose religion you do not know.
examples: Happy holidays! Thanks for shopping with us.
"Happy holidays," the mail carrier said, handing over a stack of cards.
Happy holidays from all of us at Bergstrom Dental.
She signs every December email "Happy holidays."
Happy holidays — see you in the new year.

entries.meaning: Said at midnight on December 31st and then for the first couple of weeks of January, to anybody you have not seen yet that year. Capital N and Y are standard when the phrase names the holiday itself.
examples: "Happy new year!" everyone shouted at midnight.
Happy New Year — hope this one treats you better than the last.
She called her parents at 12:01. "Happy new year, Mom."
Happy new year to you and yours.
It's the eighteenth of January and he's still saying happy new year to everybody.

entries.meaning: The greeting for the fourth Thursday in November, said on the day and for a few days on either side of it. It is the one big American holiday formula with no religious edge at all, which is why offices and cashiers use it freely where they would hedge with happy holidays in December.
examples: "Happy Thanksgiving!" she called through the screen door, holding a pie.
Happy Thanksgiving — drive safe, and call when you get in.
He said happy Thanksgiving to the whole crew and sent everybody home at noon.
"Happy Turkey Day," her brother texted, with a photo of the fryer.
Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at the station.

variants: many happy returns of the day
entries.meaning: An old birthday wish — that the day may come back many more times — still ordinary in Britain and distinctly antique in the United States. An American who says it is usually being courtly on purpose or quoting a grandparent.
examples: "Many happy returns," he wrote inside the card.
Many happy returns of the day, my dear.
Great-Aunt Ruth still sends a note every year wishing me many happy returns.
"Happy birthday!" "And many happy returns," her husband added.
Many happy returns, Professor. We hope there are eighty more.

entries.meaning: Hebrew and Yiddish for good fortune, said as congratulations at weddings, bar and bat mitzvahs, births, and graduations. It is understood well beyond Jewish American communities, and it congratulates an accomplished fact rather than wishing future luck.
examples: "Mazel tov!" the guests shouted as the glass broke.
Mazel tov on the engagement — we're thrilled for you.
He hugged his son. "Mazel tov, kiddo."
Mazel tov to the graduate and to the parents who paid for it.
"She got in early decision." "Mazel tov!"

entries.meaning: The standard Christmas greeting in American English. Note merry, not happy — this is the one holiday that takes a different adjective, and it simply has to be memorized.
examples: Merry Christmas! Come in, come in.
"Merry Christmas, Mrs. Delgado," the kids called from the sidewalk.
Merry Christmas and a happy new year.
He said merry Christmas to every single person in the checkout line.
Merry Christmas, everybody — and don't peek at the presents.

entries.meaning: A blessing on the dead, carved on headstones and now the standard way Americans mark a death online. The abbreviation RIP is normally spelled out letter by letter in speech, occasionally read as the word rip, and it has spread jokingly to broken phones and canceled shows.
examples: Rest in peace, Grandma. We'll miss you every single day.
"RIP to a legend," the post read.
He was a good dog. Rest easy, buddy.
RIP my laptop, 2014 to 2026.
She was ninety-two, and she went in her sleep. May she rest in peace.

entries.ipa: /ˌsɑri fər jər ˈlɔs/, also /ˌsɔri fər jər ˈlɔs/
entries.meaning: The default American condolence to someone who has been bereaved — expected, safe, and slightly impersonal, which is exactly why police officers, coworkers, and anyone who did not know the deceased reach for it. Nobody will fault you for saying it, and nobody will remember that you did.
examples: "I'm so sorry for your loss," the officer said quietly.
Sorry for your loss, man. Anything you need, you call me.
Every card in the stack said some version of sorry for your loss.
"I heard about your mom. I'm sorry for your loss."
He shook every hand in the receiving line: "Sorry for your loss. Sorry for your loss."

variants: our thoughts and prayers are with you
thoughts and prayers to the family
entries.meaning: An offer of sympathy after a death, an illness, or a disaster. Said to one grieving person it is sincere and ordinary; issued publicly after a mass shooting it has been mocked so relentlessly as a substitute for action that many Americans now hear it as empty by default.
examples: "You and your family are in our thoughts and prayers."
Thoughts and prayers to everyone still without power tonight.
She sent flowers and a note: thoughts and prayers.
Another press conference, another round of thoughts and prayers, and nothing changes.
"Thoughts and prayers," he said, and you could hear the quotation marks around it.

entries.meaning: Arabic for praise be to God, and the everyday Muslim response to good news, to how are you?, and to a finished meal. In American English it does exactly the work that thank God and praise the Lord do, and among Arab and Muslim Americans it is just as frequent and just as unremarkable.
examples: "How've you been?" "Good, alhamdulillah."
The biopsy came back clean. Alhamdulillah.
He pushed back from the table. "Alhamdulillah. I can't eat another bite."
Alhamdulillah — everybody got out of the building.
She says hamdulillah where her coworkers say thank God, and it means the same thing.

entries.meaning: Hebrew for so be it, said at the close of a prayer to affirm it. Outside church it is one of the most common ways an American endorses a statement — amen to that means I could not possibly agree more. Both pronunciations are standard; ay-MEN is more common in Protestant and gospel settings, ah-MEN in Catholic liturgy and in secular agreement.
examples: "...in Jesus' name we pray. Amen."
Amen, and pass the potatoes.
"This week needs to be over." "Amen to that."
Amen, brother. Preach.
The whole congregation answered amen.
Nobody should have to work on their own birthday. — Amen.

entries.meaning: An old devotional exclamation of wonder or thanks, and also the name of a short Catholic prayer. In everyday American speech it is antique, rural, and often faintly comic — a grandmother's version of wow.
examples: "Glory be, would you look at that."
Glory be to God, the boy finally cleaned his room.
She stepped out onto the porch. "Glory be, it's snowing."
Glory be — the truck started on the first try.
My grandmother says glory be about eleven times a day.

entries.meaning: A ward set against a bad possibility, dropped in immediately after naming it — the dark twin of knock on wood. Most Americans who say it are asking God for no more than they are when they say bless you. Said with the weight on forbid, it flips into sarcasm and mocks somebody else's overreaction.
examples: If anything happens to me, God forbid, the will is in the safe.
God forbid the man should ever admit he took a wrong turn.
We'd need a bigger generator if the power went out for a week, God forbid.
Heaven forbid we start a meeting on time around here.
"What if she says no?" "God forbid. Then we're back to square one."

entries.meaning: Hebrew for praise the Lord, used in worship and, far more often in daily speech, as an exclamation of relief that something has finally happened. The spelling alleluia is the Latin-derived church form.
examples: "Hallelujah!" the choir sang.
The heat's back on. Hallelujah.
Hallelujah — she finally answered her phone.
"The results came back negative." "Hallelujah."
He threw up both hands. "Hallelujah, it's Friday."

entries.meaning: Arabic for if God wills it, attached to any statement about the future. It is everyday speech for Muslim and Arab Americans and completely sincere; among people outside those communities it has also picked up a joking second life meaning that is never happening on schedule.
examples: "See you at the wedding in June." "Inshallah."
We close on the house next month, inshallah.
God willing, she'll be home from the hospital by Friday.
"Is the plumber actually coming today?" "Inshallah."
He ends every plan with inshallah, and he means every word of it.

entries.meaning: Arabic for what God has willed, said while admiring something — a baby, a new house, somebody's good news. It gives the credit to God, and in long practice it also keeps the compliment from drawing the evil eye. Leaving it out when you praise a child can genuinely sting in Arab and Muslim American families, which makes it one of the few formulas here where the omission is the message.
examples: "Look how big he's gotten!" "Mashallah."
Mashallah, the house came out beautiful.
She showed her aunt the acceptance letter and got "mashallah" four separate times.
Three languages at six years old, mashallah.
He complimented the baby without saying mashallah, and his mother-in-law noticed.

entries.meaning: The blessing exchanged during the sign of peace at Mass and in many Protestant services, said while shaking hands with the people around you. Outside a church it is deliberately solemn, and among friends it is gently ironic.
examples: He turned to the pew behind him. "Peace be with you."
"Peace be with you." "And with your spirit."
The priest raised his hand: "Peace be with you all."
She ended the eulogy with "peace be with you" and stepped down from the lectern.
"Peace be with you, brother," he said, handing the wrench back.

entries.meaning: A short devotional thanks to God, now heard mostly from older and more religious speakers and in historical settings — and, since The Handmaid's Tale, with an ominous edge for younger listeners. Secular Americans use it ironically.
examples: "Praise be," she said when the rain finally came.
Everybody got home safe, praise be.
Praise be to God for another harvest.
The printer works again. Praise be.
"Praise be," he muttered, watching the tow truck finally pull in.

variants: praise the Lord and pass the ammunition
entries.meaning: A devotional exclamation of thanks and joy, standard in American church speech and especially in Black and evangelical churches, where it works as call and response. In secular mouths it is relief laid on thick.
examples: "Praise the Lord!" somebody shouted from the back pew.
She came through the surgery just fine. Praise God.
Praise the Lord — the check finally cleared.
"Praise the Lord," said the pastor, "and amen."
He got the job. Praise the Lord.

entries.meaning: Called out by whoever is faster when two people say the same thing at the same instant. The playground rules — the loser owes a soda and cannot speak until somebody says their name — are known to every American child and get invoked, half-seriously, by adults forever after.
examples: They both said "pizza" in the same breath. "Jinx!"
"Jinx, you owe me a Coke."
"That's exactly what I was about to say." "Jinx. You can't talk now."
Two of us called jinx at the same moment, which the rules do not cover.
He mouthed jinx across the conference table and went back to his notes.

entries.meaning: What the person holding the camera says a half second before the shutter, because the word pulls the mouth into a smile. The scripted answer is the word cheese, stretched out until the picture is taken.
examples: "Everybody squeeze in. Say cheese!"
Say cheese — and Grandpa, open your eyes this time.
"Say cheese." "Cheeeeese."
He counted to three, said say cheese, and took the picture a beat too early anyway.
Twenty relatives on a staircase, saying cheese for the fourth time.

variants: trick or treat, smell my feet
entries.meaning: What American children shout at the door on Halloween to ask for candy; the threatened "trick" is entirely theoretical. Adults say it jokingly when they turn up anywhere hoping to be handed something.
examples: "Trick or treat!" three small ghosts shouted through the screen door.
She opened the door with the bowl ready. "Trick or treat, huh?"
Trick or treat — and please, not raisins again this year.
He knocked on his neighbor's door holding an empty casserole dish. "Trick or treat."
The kids practiced saying trick or treat the whole way down the block.
